absent: Acquisition mechanics and capacity of per-CPU callchain entries and recursion contexts beyond balanced release.
Kernel and user stack walking mechanics and context marker encoding.
Layout and lifetime of uprobe return instances and XOL areas beyond trampoline address lookup.
Default values for callchain depth and context limits and numeric value behind six_hundred_forty_kb.
PMU registration, scheduling, and side-band handling beyond global counters, masks, and locks.
SMP invocation, sysctl registration, atomic, lockdep, IRQ flag, and math helper internals owned by other dossiers.
Perf context scheduling, cgroup info layout, time array indices, and sibling iteration mechanics.
Early console registration and write semantics beyond null check and bounded emit.
IRQ work lifecycle for duration warnings and max_samples_per_tick management beyond throttling updates.
Group leader state values and transitions beyond effective-state deferral.

findings.text: A helper reports the trampoline location associated with the current address space for user probes, returning a defined no-trampoline sentinel when no execution area is present. Callers use it to recognize trampoline artifacts in captured addresses.

Combined callchain capture serves kernel and user requests under explicit limits. It guarantees null for unsupported cross-task user-only capture and for acquisition failure, and guarantees balanced release of per-CPU recursion protection on every return path including early exits.

Capture eligibility depends on privilege and flags. Kernel capture applies only in kernel privilege. User capture originating in kernel privilege resolves to the current task and is abandoned for non-user tasks. A deferred cookie request records dedicated markers instead of copying user memory.

User captures overlapping pending user return probes carry a bounded substitution contract. Only newly appended addresses are examined, each trampoline occurrence is replaced by the corresponding saved original return address in list order, and the scan stops at capture end or exhaustion of pending instances.

Administrative control for callchain depth and context limits. Read and parse failures propagate without side effects, while a successful write is serialized and rejected as busy when callchain consumers are active, otherwise updating the stored limit.

Callchain administration publishes under kernel an entry named perf_event_max_stack and an entry named perf_event_max_contexts_per_stack, each with mode 0644. The stack entry is bounded below by SYSCTL_ZERO and above by six_hundred_forty_kb. The contexts entry is bounded below by SYSCTL_ZERO and above by SYSCTL_ONE_THOUSAND. Registration happens at early init.
A cross-CPU request descriptor associates an optional target task with a callback pointer, an opaque argument, and an integer outcome slot preset by the initiator to a retry or absence code.
An event-targeted work descriptor binds a perf event to a handler that operates on CPU and task contexts plus opaque data, used to transport the request to the owning location.

A scoped lock guard pairs a per-CPU context pointer with an optional task context pointer. Construction acquires the pair and destruction releases the pair, supporting automatic cleanup on scope exit.

Cross-CPU invocation executes a callback on a chosen processor or on the processor currently running a chosen task. Task-targeted dispatch tolerates migration by retrying with voluntary scheduling between attempts, while CPU-targeted dispatch performs a single synchronous attempt.

Remote dispatch distinguishes migration retry from wrong task and from absent processor or task. The callee side validates execution on the expected processor and, when a task is named, validates identity with the current task before running the callback.

Context activity encoding uses distinct bits. Symbol EVENT_FLEXIBLE has value 1. Symbol EVENT_PINNED has value 2. Symbol EVENT_TIME has value 4. Symbol EVENT_FROZEN has value 8. Symbol EVENT_CPU has value 16. Symbol EVENT_CGROUP has value 32. Symbol EVENT_GUEST has value 64. Groupings combine cgroup with guest as flags, flexible with pinned as all, and time with frozen as time-frozen.

Perf context protection uses raw spinlocks with fixed order of per-CPU context before task context when both are present, and reverse release. Acquisition warns if the frozen marker is already present. Release clears the frozen marker, with full reset when no scheduling flags remain.

A reserved pointer value of negative one denotes a tombstoned task. Kernel-owned events are recognized by that owner marker. The accessor for the current processor task context requires disabled interrupts and returns the per-CPU stored task context.

Event-specific dispatch routes a handler to the owner of the event context. Processor-owned events run on the recorded processor. Task-owned events run on the task processor when active, otherwise the initiator falls back to direct local execution under locks after revalidating tombstone and activity state.

Event dispatch holds the per-CPU lock and, for task events, the associated task context lock while invoking the handler, with interrupts disabled on local paths. Non-child events require the context mutex to stabilize the event to context association. Tombstoned tasks cause immediate return without invoking the handler.

Accepted option bits are the union of individual symbols PERF_FLAG_FD_NO_GROUP plus PERF_FLAG_FD_OUTPUT plus PERF_FLAG_PID_CGROUP plus PERF_FLAG_FD_CLOEXEC. Privileged branch sampling permission is the union of PERF_SAMPLE_BRANCH_KERNEL plus PERF_SAMPLE_BRANCH_HV.

Scheduler integration state comprises a disabled-by-default static key, a dedicated mutex with reference count, per-CPU side-band event lists, and separate read-mostly atomic usage counters for mmap, comm, namespaces, task, frequency, switch, ksymbol, BPF, cgroup, text poke, and build identifier classes.
PMU registry mutation serializes on a dedicated mutex with SRCU protection for readers. Scheduler accounting mutation serializes on a separate dedicated mutex.

Topology-aware online tracking provides separate CPU masks for aggregate, core, die, cluster, package, and system scope. Event allocation uses a dedicated slab cache. Per-CPU perf processor context instances anchor scheduling state.

Guest context load is tracked by a per-CPU boolean with an accessor reporting the current processor value. An alternate build configuration provides the same accessor unconditionally reporting false, indicating absence of mediated guest support.

Default perf controls are paranoid level 2, maximum sample rate 100000, sample period of one second divided by that rate, maximum CPU time 25 percent, and allowed sample cost as period scaled by percent over 100 with minimum 1. Mlock allowance defaults to 512 plus page size in kilobytes.

Sample rate and CPU time limit controls validate writes against throttling state, recompute per-tick allowance and period on success, and warn while disabling the allowance when throttling is turned off via 0 or 100 percent.

Core perf administration publishes under kernel four entries with mode 0644. One is named perf_event_paranoid. One is named perf_event_mlock_kb. One is named perf_event_max_sample_rate bounded below by SYSCTL_ONE. One is named perf_cpu_time_max_percent bounded by SYSCTL_ZERO and SYSCTL_ONE_HUNDRED. The paranoid entry is a compatibility commitment that user space may probe and that implementers must retain.

Interrupt cost regulation maintains a per-CPU decaying accumulator over 128 samples. When the smoothed average exceeds the allowed budget, the subsystem lowers effective sample rate and per-tick limit, records diagnostic values for a rate-limited warning, and prefers deferred warning work with an early console fallback if queuing fails. Zero allowance disables regulation.

Early boot textual output formats a variable argument message into a 512 byte bounded buffer with truncation and emits it through the registered early console when present, otherwise performing no action.

Event identity draws from a global 64 bit atomic counter. Debug printing defaults to a weak no-operation hook. Time sources are the local clock for generic stamps and a per-event clock callback for event stamps.

Effective event state defers to the group leader when the leader is off or worse, otherwise reflects the member state. Enabled time accrues from inactive upward and running time accrues from active upward, each as prior totals plus elapsed time since the last stamp, with group-wide sibling refresh available.

Event time lookup returns zero for events without a context, delegates cgroup events to per-CPU cgroup timing, and otherwise reads total context time minus guest time when the event excludes guest execution.

Two build configurations define cgroup event handling. The enabled variant recognizes events by non-null cgroup association and reads per-CPU cgroup timing for the event processor, while the disabled variant reports no cgroup events and zero cgroup time.

Recursion and concurrency risks include leaking per-CPU callchain protection on missed release, racing task migration during cross-CPU dispatch, invoking event handlers on the wrong task or processor if validation is skipped, and dereferencing tombstoned task pointers.

Configuration risks include changing depth or rate limits while consumers are active, disabling interrupt throttling which risks system unresponsiveness, and underestimating smoothed cost until enough samples have accumulated.

Locking and interrupt risks include acquiring task context before processor context, sleeping while holding raw context spinlocks, running local event paths with interrupts enabled, and clearing frozen state while scheduling flags remain.
